items.title: DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

items.title: DOC/ENH: StandardScaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

items.title: Incorrect random_state description in RANSACRegressor documentation
items.body: ### Introduce yourself Hi! I am new to the scikit-learn community. I am a data scientist and often use `scikit-learn` for my experiments. I recently used `RANSACRegressor` and noticed a possible documentation issue. ### Describe the issue linked to the documentation The `random_state` parameter is currently documented as: `The generator used to initialize the centers`. This description appears unrelated to `RANSACRegressor` and actually related to a clustering algorithm . In the implementation, `random_state` is used with `sample_without_replacement` to randomly select data subsets during RANSAC iterations. These subsets are then used to fit candidate models. The issue also stays in the final `sklearn` documentation linked here : [ransac](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.RANSACRegressor.html. ### Suggest a potential alternative/fix Suggested correction : `random_state : int, RandomState instance, default=None Controls the randomness of the data subsets selected during RANSAC iterations. Pass an int for reproducible output across multiple function calls. See :term:`Glossary `.` I have tested the change locally, and the RANSAC test suite passes: 27 passed in 0.47s I would be happy to submit a pull request for this documentation fix if the issue is valid.

items.title: Clarify parameter/hyperparameter terminology in the cross-validation workflow diagram
items.body:
### Introduce yourself

I teach machine learning engineering to people who are new to machine learning.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

I use `GridSearchCV` to help learners understand grid search, model selection, and good practice. I think it is a fantastic teaching tool, and the user guide is excellent.

I've taught this section several times and have repeatedly needed to explain why the diagram says "parameters" when we are discussing hyperparameters. This is a recurring point of confusion in my teaching, which prompted this issue.

The overall workflow diagram in the cross-validation user guide uses the labels **"Parameters"** and **"Best parameters"**.

User guide:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html

Direct link to the diagram:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/grid_search_workflow.png

My learners are meeting the terms "parameter" and "hyperparameter" for the first time. They are still learning the difference between settings we specify or search over, such as a decision tree's maximum depth, and values the model learns during fitting.

When I explain grid search, I describe it as comparing hyperparameter settings. The diagram calls these "Parameters" and "Best parameters". I then have to explain why the same settings are being called by two different names, while learners are still trying to understand what those names mean.

I understand that scikit-learn uses "parameters" for estimator constructor settings. The glossary explains this convention:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The cross-validation guide also uses the word "hyperparameters". A short explanation at the diagram would help beginners connect the two terms.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Could a short note be added beside or below the diagram to explain how "parameters" relates to "hyperparameters"? For example:

> Here, "parameters" means configurable estimator settings. These can include machine-learning hyperparameters, such as a decision tree's `max_depth`, as well as other configuration choices, such as which estimator or pipeline step to use. They are different from values learned by the model during fitting.

The note could link to the glossary:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The diagram could keep its existing labels. The note would help beginners understand why settings such as `max_depth` may be called "hyperparameters" in machine-learning terminology while scikit-learn uses the broader term "parameters".

items.title: Documentation: Incorrect description of statistic computed by MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Pradip, a Computer Engineering student and I’m currently learning and working with Python and machine learning. I use scikit-learn for learning and implementing machine learning algorithms and preprocessing techniques.

While going through the `MaxAbsScaler` documentation and source code, I noticed a discrepancy in the `partial_fit()` docstring. I’m opening this issue to clarify the documentation and make it consistent with the actual implementation.


### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` currently states that the data is used to compute the **"per-feature minimum and maximum"**.

However, `MaxAbsScaler` computes the **maximum absolute value** for each feature and stores it in `max_abs_`.

For example:

```python
X = [[-2, 5],
     [-3, 1]]
```

For the first feature:

```text
minimum = -3
maximum = -2
maximum absolute value = 3
```

`MaxAbsScaler` uses `3` as the scaling value. It does not use the minimum and maximum as separate statistics.

The implementation reflects this:

```python
max_abs = xpx.nanmax(xp.abs(X), axis=0, xp=xp)
```

Therefore, the current wording may confuse users into thinking that `MaxAbsScaler` computes and uses both the minimum and maximum values independently.

This also appears inconsistent with the class-level documentation, which describes the scaler in terms of the **maximum absolute value**.

I believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm.


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I suggest updating the `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` from:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

to:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

This would make the `partial_fit()` documentation accurately reflect the statistic computed by the implementation and remain consistent with the class-level documentation.

items.title: SelectFromModel's `prefit` fails unless fit is called when set_output(transform="pandas")
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

My understanding is that if `prefit`is true, one could, in principle call `transform()` without calling `fit()` first.

While this is true if we don't set the output to pandas, it fails when we do so:

Minimal reproduction:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel

X, y = load_iris(as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)

# prefit=True -- docs say we don't need to call .fit() on sel
sel = SelectFromModel(clf, prefit=True).set_output(transform="pandas")

sel.transform(X)
```

```
NotFittedError: This SelectFromModel instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this estimator.
```

Without `.set_output(transform="pandas")`, the identical `prefit=True` selector transforms `X` just fine with no `.fit()` call. 

The error only appears once pandas output is requested, because `set_output` internally calls `get_feature_names_out()`, which checks whether the *wrapper itself* has been fitted (via `check_is_fitted(self)`, not `check_is_fitted(self.estimator)`). 

According to Claude, that check was intentionally added in #25308 to standardize `get_feature_names_out()` behavior across `SelectorMixin` estimators.

So my question is: is this expected behaviour? or is it an unintended bug? 

From a user perspective, if I use `fit`again, even though prefit is True, I get the impression that my estimator would be re-fitted, so if this is intended, it might be worth adding a line in the docs.

```python
sel.fit(X, y)     # with prefit=True, does NOT retrain clf -- just
                  # deep-copies it and records feature_names_in_
sel.transform(X)  # now works
```

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

SelectFromModel's prefit parameter is documented as:

prefit : bool, default=False
Whether a prefit model is expected to be passed into the constructor directly or not. If True, estimator must be a fitted estimator. If False, estimator is fitted and updated by calling fit and partial_fit, respectively.

Maybe it's just me, but I sort of read this as, if the estimator is prefit, I could avoid calling fit and it would be just fine.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a note to the prefit parameter docstring, e.g.:

Note: even with prefit=True, .fit() must still be called before using get_feature_names_out() or set_output(transform="pandas"), since these check whether the selector itself (not the underlying estimator) has been fitted. Calling .fit() in this case does not refit estimator; it only records bookkeeping metadata (estimator_, feature_names_in_).

items.title: BIC-based model selection in plot_gmm_selection.py silently picks the wrong model under anisotropy severe enough to break its own initialization
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## Describe the issue linked to the documentation

`examples/mixture/plot_gmm_selection.py` demonstrates using `GridSearchCV` + BIC to select `n_components` and `covariance_type` for a `GaussianMixture`. It works well on the example's data because the two components are already well separated relative to their own spread, so `GaussianMixture`'s default k-means-style initialization lands close to the true partition and EM refines it correctly.

As in [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), that init dependency is invisible in the example and doesn't generalize. If the true clusters are anisotropic enough that Euclidean-distance-based initialization is already unreliable, BIC does not fail loudly -- it fails silently, by scoring every candidate in the grid on a bad fit and confidently reporting the best of a bad set. A reader walks away with "BIC picked `n_components=2`, full covariance, done" with no signal that a different initialization would have picked a different, better-scoring model entirely.

Concretely, on two anisotropic "parallel cigars" clusters (`make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, same construction as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), ratio 4x rather than 80x), the grid search over `n_components` and `covariance_type` with default initialization selects a 3-component model, when the true generative model has 2 components. The 2-component model is available in the same search space -- it's just never found, because every restart of k-means++ on this data lands in roughly the same wrong place.

## Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a new section to `plot_gmm_selection.py`, after the existing example, showing:

1. The same "parallel cigars" dataset as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), where default (raw) k-means-style initialization for `GaussianMixture` gives a partition bad enough that BIC-based model selection lands on the wrong `n_components`.
2. A whitened-init variant: use `PCA(whiten=True)` + `KMeans` only to get an initial cluster assignment, derive `weights_init`/`means_init` from that assignment on the raw data, then fit and score every model (whitened-init or not) by BIC on the raw data. This keeps the BIC comparison valid while showing that whitening the initialization -- not the model itself -- restores the correct selection.

Draft implementation, for review before opening a PR: https://github.com/jovo/scikit-learn/pull/2 (this is a fork-internal PR against my own fork, not yet a real PR against `scikit-learn/scikit-learn` -- opening one once there's agreement this is worth doing, per the guidance on [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842)).

items.title: GaussianMixture is not a universal fix for anisotropy — plot_kmeans_assumptions.py doesn't show the case where whitening is needed too
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

`examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_assumptions.py` shows `KMeans` failing on anisotropic blobs and proposes `GaussianMixture` as the fix, since it fits a full covariance per component instead of assuming spherical clusters.

That's correct for the anisotropy shown in the example, but not universally: `GaussianMixture` is still initialized from a k-means-style partition of the raw data, and EM only ever *refines* that partition rather than searching from scratch. If the anisotropy is severe enough, the initial partition can already be too wrong for EM to recover from, even with unconstrained covariances.

**What a reader might do without knowing this:** someone hits poor `KMeans` results on their own anisotropic data, finds this example, and takes away the rule "if k-means struggles with anisotropy, switch to `GaussianMixture`." They swap it in, `GaussianMixture` returns *some* clustering with no error or warning, and they ship it — never realizing the result can be arbitrarily wrong, because their anisotropy happened to be severe enough to also break the initialization this fix silently depends on. Nothing in the current example signals that this failure mode exists, so there's no reason for them to suspect it.

I'd like to propose adding: a more severely anisotropic dataset (built the same way as the file's existing `X_aniso` — `make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, just more extreme) where `GaussianMixture` fails (ARI ≈ 0), and where whitening first with `PCA(whiten=True)` fixes it (ARI ≈ 0.9+) — no custom clustering code needed, just a change of input to the same `GaussianMixture` call.

(Caveat: this degrades in high dimension too — same construction at d=30, ARI drops back to ≈0.)

Draft implementation, kept up to date: jovo/scikit-learn#1 (opened against my own fork so it stays open and reviewable rather than getting auto-closed like a direct PR here would while this issue is pending triage — happy to open a PR against this repo once there's agreement this is worth doing).

items.title: Document tie-breaking behavior for max_categories in OneHotEncoder/OrdinalEncoder infrequent category grouping
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation



When `max_categories` forces additional categories into the infrequent group beyond what `min_frequency` alone would select, and multiple categories are tied in count at the cutoff boundary, the docs for `max_categories` don't specify which tied category is kept as frequent vs. grouped as infrequent.

Looking at `_identify_infrequent()` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, the tie-break is implicit rather than documented:

```python
# stable sort to preserve original count order
smallest_levels = np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")[:-frequent_category_count]
infrequent_mask[smallest_levels] = True
```

Counts are sorted using `np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")` — a stable sort — so ties are resolved by the order categories appear in `categories_[i]`, which for `categories='auto'` is lexicographic/numeric sort order. This behavior is not mentioned in the `max_categories` docstring or the User Guide section on infrequent categories (`encoder_infrequent_categories`).

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a sentence to the `max_categories` parameter docs (in both `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder`) and to the User Guide section on infrequent categories, stating that ties in category count are broken using the sort order of the categories (via a stable sort). This is also relevant to the discussion in #32161.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

X = np.array([["a"] * 2 + ["b"] * 2 + ["c"] * 5], dtype=object).T
enc = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=2, sparse_output=False).fit(X)
print(enc.infrequent_categories_)
# 'a' and 'b' tie at count=2 -- which one is grouped as infrequent
# is not documented, though it is deterministic.
```

### Additional context

Related: #32161 discusses tie-breaking by lexicographical order for encoder category ordering more broadly.

items.title: DOC: Array API - mention torch XPU is a bit unstable
items.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

While running tests and benchmarks with scikit-learn Array API backed by torch XPU, I got many errors:
- float precision (fixed in 2.12)
- JIT hangs (fixed in 2.13)
- And other kind of hang and a very bad slowdown for some matmul: https://github.com/intel/torch-xpu-ops/issues/4805 (hang fixed in upcoming 2.14, but not the slowdown).

I got none of such errors with dpnp backed tests/runs.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

At least mention torch XPU is still a bit unstable and that users are encouraged to use the latest versions (fixes are being made quickly).

And maybe mention that dpnp is more robust as of august 2026. Though it might also be slower, I'll have some benchmark results soon.

This is not urgent to fix, I'm opening this issue to keep track of things. We can wait for some benchmark results before editing the array API doc.

items.title: DOC: Add table to Recommendation Summary section in Common Pitfalls
items.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

In the [controlling pitfalls](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html) page, in section 12.3, there is a recommendation summary for controlling randomness. I feel that while the note is okay, it makes sense to keep something simple to improve readability for beginners who need an easy reference to look at.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a table to the recommendation summary section, below the paragraph. This will make it really easy for people to have an idea about some scenarios that they may run into and what they should handle. What I have so far is:

| Goal | Estimator | CV Splitter|
| ----- | ---- | ---- |
|  Same results every fit/split call  | int  | int |
| Robust CV of a randomized estimator (fresh RNG per fold) | RandomState or None   | int    |
| Comparable fold-to-fold scores across separate runs   | (any)  | int |
| Reproducible across program executions  | fixed RandomState or int | int |

Let me know if this is a good idea or there are any changes/additions to the table!

items.title: Explicit documentation / contract for free-threading

labels.name: free-threading
labels.description: PRs and issues related to support for free-threaded CPython (a.k.a. nogil or no-GIL, PEP 703)

items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Scikit-learn offers builds for free-threaded Python, but it is not clear as a user what is supposed to be safe to call from multiple threads.

For example, it feels quite obvious that one should not call `.fit()` on the same object from multiple threads even if not documented, but does the interface guarantee that other methods are safe to call on the same object from multiple threads? For instance, KNN depending on the arguments might do most of the work in other methods, and I'm not sure if it doesn't modify any internal attributes starting with underscores.

Further, since lots of other Python libraries offer scikit-learn-compatible objects, it would be quite useful to have official documentation from scikit-learn about what needs or doesn't need to be thread-safe in order to develop scikit-learn-compatible classes.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a documentation page for free threading covering all these kinds of details, plus additional documentation on a per-estimator basis if needed for exceptions. Mention these thread safety requirements also in the developer guide.

items.title: DOC: clarify n_iter_ can be 0 when warm_start=True in LogisticRegression
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

When using `LogisticRegression` with `warm_start=True`, the `n_iter_` 
attribute reports `[0]` on subsequent fits if the model has already 
converged:

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=4, random_state=0)

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, warm_start=True, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [7]
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [0] — unexpected for users
```

This is technically correct — lbfgs needs 0 iterations when starting 
from an already-optimal point — but it is surprising and undocumented.

### Suggested fix

Add a note to the `n_iter_` attribute docstring mentioning that 
`n_iter_` can be 0 when `warm_start=True` and the model has already 
converged from a previous fit.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

items.title: [DOC] Improve docstring for `orthogonal_mp`
items.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

Currently, the [rendered documentation for `linear_model.orthogonal_mp`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp.html#sklearn.linear_model.orthogonal_mp) ([source](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/cc50648cc1b759b53a4edbce0f3bb6c237349448/sklearn/linear_model/_omp.py#L316-L324)) is missing a formalism and the included LaTeX is not rendered. 

Further, looking at the included formalisms, it seems that the notation is changed between this docstring and [the User Guide section on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html#orthogonal-matching-pursuit-omp), which uses a _w_ rather than a _gamma_.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I see two potential fixes:

1.  Updating the docstring formatting and notation. I would suggest standardizing this with what's currently in the User Guide :

```
    Solves `n_targets` Orthogonal Matching Pursuit problems.
    Each instance of the problem aims to approximate the optimum solution vector, parametrized by the number of non-zero coefficients using
    `n_nonzero_coefs`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||y - Xw||^2_2 \text{subject to} ||w||_0 <= n_{nonzero coefs}

    When parametrized by error using the parameter `tol`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||w||_0 \text{subject to} ||y - Xw||^2_2 <= tol
```

2. Removing this portion of the docstring to direct users towards the formalism in the User Guide, as is done for `linear_model.OrthogonalMatchingPursuit`.

I'm happy to open a PR with either fix !

items.title: DOC: fix typo and inconsistencies in RidgeClassifier docstrings
items.body:
### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py`, there are several docstring issues 
in the Ridge classifier classes:

**1. Typo in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`**

Current:
    X : {array-like, spare matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)

Should be:
    X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)

**2. Extra space in `Ridge` See Also section**

Current:
    RidgeClassifierCV :  Ridge classifier with built-in cross validation.

Should be:
    RidgeClassifierCV : Ridge classifier with built-in cross validation.

**3. Missing RST function links in `RidgeClassifier` solver descriptions**

`Ridge` correctly uses RST `:func:` links for solver references:
    'cholesky' uses the standard :func:`scipy.linalg.solve` function
    'sparse_cg' uses :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.cg`
    'lsqr' uses :func:`scipy.sparse.linalg.lsqr`

But `RidgeClassifier` describes the same solvers as plain text without 
`:func:` links, making the documentation inconsistent.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/linear_model/_ridge.py` and search for:
- `spare matrix` in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`
- Double space after colon in the See Also section of `Ridge`
- The solver descriptions in `RidgeClassifier` vs `Ridge`

### Suggested fix

- Fix `spare` → `sparse` in `_RidgeClassifierMixin.predict`
- Remove extra space in See Also section
- Add `:func:` RST links to solver descriptions in `RidgeClassifier`

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/ensemble/_weight_boosting.py`, there are several grammatical 
errors and inconsistencies in the docstrings of `AdaBoostClassifier` 
and `AdaBoostRegressor`:

**1. Missing word in module docstring**

Current:
    This module structure is the following:

Should be:
    The module structure is as follows:

**2. Grammar error in `decision_function` and `staged_decision_function`**

Current (appears multiple times):
    Binary classification is a special cases with ``k == 1``

Should be:
    Binary classification is a special case with ``k == 1``

**3. Grammar error in `staged_decision_function`, `staged_predict_proba`**

Current (appears multiple times):
    The order of outputs is the same of that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.

Should be:
    The order of outputs is the same as that of the :term:`classes_` attribute.

**4. Grammar error in reference citation in `AdaBoostRegressor`**

Current:
    An AdaBoost [1] regressor

Should be:
    An AdaBoost [1]_ regressor

Note: `AdaBoostClassifier` correctly uses `[1]_` with the trailing 
underscore for RST citation syntax, but `AdaBoostRegressor` is missing it.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/ensemble/_weight_boosting.py` and search for the phrases above.

### Suggested fix

Fix the grammatical errors and citation syntax as described above.
